label: Curvature and Topology
notes: This capstone chapter spans printed pages 345 to 370 and asks how local curvature constrains global shape. We collect the great comparison theorems: Cartan-Hadamard for nonpositive curvature, Bonnet-Myers and Synge for positive curvature, Killing-Hopf for constant curvature, and the sphere theorem for pinched positive curvature.

label: The Guiding Question
notes: Curvature is computed from second derivatives of the metric, a purely local quantity, yet it forces facts about the whole manifold. We frame the chapter as a dictionary translating the sign of curvature into statements about the fundamental group, the diffeomorphism type, and compactness of a complete Riemannian manifold.

label: A Map of the Theorems
notes: This map keys each theorem to the sign of curvature. Negative or nonpositive curvature spreads geodesics apart and yields aspherical Cartan-Hadamard manifolds. Positive curvature focuses geodesics, forcing compactness through Bonnet-Myers and roundness through the sphere theorem. Constant curvature pins down the universal cover exactly via Killing-Hopf.

label: Cartan-Hadamard Theorem
notes: For a complete, simply connected manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature, the exponential map at any point is a diffeomorphism onto the whole manifold. Such a Hadamard manifold is therefore diffeomorphic to Euclidean space, has no conjugate points, and every two points are joined by a unique minimizing geodesic.

label: Why the Exponential Map Wins
notes: Nonpositive curvature makes Jacobi fields grow at least linearly, so they never vanish away from the origin and conjugate points cannot occur. The exponential map is then a local diffeomorphism everywhere; completeness and simple connectivity upgrade this to a global covering, hence a diffeomorphism onto the manifold.

label: Topology of Nonpositive Curvature
notes: Because a complete nonpositively curved manifold has Euclidean universal cover, it is aspherical: all higher homotopy groups vanish. Its fundamental group carries the entire homotopy type, the manifold is a classifying space, and torsion in that group is forbidden, sharply restricting which spaces admit such metrics.

label: Constant Curvature and Killing-Hopf
notes: Cartan's local-to-global theorem shows that complete simply connected manifolds of the same constant curvature are isometric. The Killing-Hopf theorem then classifies every complete constant-curvature manifold as a quotient of the sphere, Euclidean space, or hyperbolic space by a discrete group of isometries acting freely.

label: The Model Space Forms
notes: Three model spaces realize constant curvature: the round sphere for positive, Euclidean space for zero, and hyperbolic space for negative curvature. Every space form is covered by exactly one of these, so understanding the three models gives a complete picture of constant-curvature geometry up to discrete quotients.

label: Bonnet-Myers Theorem
notes: If the Ricci curvature is bounded below by a positive constant, Myers theorem bounds the diameter and forces the manifold to be compact with finite fundamental group. Positive Ricci curvature makes geodesics develop conjugate points within a fixed length, so no geodesic can minimize beyond the diameter bound.

label: Synge and Orientability
notes: Synge's theorem refines the positive-curvature story using the second variation along closed geodesics. An even-dimensional, orientable, compact manifold of positive sectional curvature is simply connected, while in odd dimensions positive curvature forces orientability, illustrating how parity of dimension enters global conclusions.

label: The Sphere Theorem
notes: The quarter-pinched sphere theorem states that a complete simply connected manifold whose sectional curvature lies in the half-open interval one-quarter to one is homeomorphic to a sphere. The pinching constant one-quarter is sharp: complex projective space with curvature in the closed interval shows the bound cannot be relaxed.

label: Curvature Obstructions and Recap
notes: We close by reading the theorems as obstructions: a torus admits no positive Ricci metric by Bonnet-Myers, and a sphere admits no nonpositive curvature metric by Cartan-Hadamard. Curvature sign therefore obstructs topology, and these capstone results convert infinitesimal bending into rigid global classification.
